title: sandhi plainly
hook: a mark you can see on the page but can't hear, and the sound of the breath
tomorrow: what did an old teacher tell students who were leaving home?

segments.voice: Yesterday, sandhi plainly and one hidden a in two schools: that, you are, or you are not that. Today a short a vanishes again, and leaves a mark nobody hears.

A rest in a piece of music is written on the page, and nobody plays it. The song still needs it. Sanskrit, written in Devanagari, has a sign like that: a small curl, a little like a stretched S, called the avagraha. In Roman letters it shows up as an apostrophe. Musicians count their rests. Readers of Sanskrit learn to see this one. Its sound? Nothing at all.
screen: `A REST NOBODY PLAYS.` → `A CURL CALLED AVAGRAHA.` → `ITS SOUND: NOTHING.`

segments.voice: The best-known place to meet it is so 'ham. Two words: sah, that one, and aham, I. First, before a short a, the -ah of sah becomes o. Then the o swallows the short a that follows. What's left is so 'ham, with the curl standing where the a used to be. Shivo 'ham, in a hymn, works the same way. The Isha Upanishad, near its end, has the full line: so 'ham asmi. That one, I am. Now say it aloud. A soft hiss, a hum, and a small gap between. Some yoga traditions hear exactly that in breathing: so riding the breath in, ham riding the breath out, a mantra the body says without being asked. They call it ajapa japa, the repetition nobody recites. Turn it around and it becomes hamsa, the swan, another name the same tradition loves. The avagraha sits in that gap. It changes nothing in the sound. On the page, it keeps a record: two words met here, and a small a let go. A reader learns to see it, and to put the a back. Sah, aham. That one, I. And the verse just before it is about seeing: the speaker asks for the golden covering over the face of truth to be drawn back, so the one who loves truth can see.
screen: `SAH + AHAM = SO 'HAM.` · `THE CURL MARKS THE DROPPED A.` · `SO IN, HAM OUT.` · then, large: `SILENT, BUT IT KEEPS A RECORD.`

segments.voice: Let the breath become just a little audible, and listen to it. On the way in there may be a soft s, on the way out something closer to a hum; if it helps, think so as the breath comes in and ham as it goes out. Notice the small gap where the breath turns. If a thought comes, let it leave on the out-breath, and come back to the sound.
Sandhi plainly: words meeting and changing. Today, an a that drops after o, and the soundless avagraha marking the spot. The curl says: something was here.
Pocket this: sandhi plainly, and even a silence on the page keeps a record. Rest well.

howItsDone: Printed Sanskrit marks a dropped a with the avagraha (ऽ), usually written as an apostrophe in Roman letters; some yoga traditions pair so with the in-breath and ham with the out-breath as a quiet repetition.

fork.setup: a friend sees shivo 'ham printed in a hymn's lyrics and asks what the apostrophe is hiding. what do you say?
options: an a: shivah plus aham, the a dropped after o.
nothing: it's a breath mark added for singers.
an h: it was shivoh ham, shortened for the tune.
fork.reveal: the same join as so 'ham: -ah becomes o, then the short a of aham drops, and the avagraha marks where it was.

original.note: Sanskrit: so 'ham, that one I am; the ऽ is the avagraha.

trapdoor: what you thought: the apostrophe is an English habit.
what it means: it stands for the avagraha, which marks a short a dropped after o.
what a scholar hears: sah + aham, the visarga becoming o, then the a elided (Ashtadhyayi 6.1.109); the avagraha records the elision and is never pronounced.
recall: that, you are; or, with atat, not
